traveler: Giovanni da Pian del Carpine (John of Plano Carpini)
title: Three Thousand Miles in a Hundred and Six Days: the Pope's Friar at the Enthronement of the Great Khan
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Umbrian Friar and the German Mission

stops.name: Pian del Carpine, a birth without a record
stops.date_confidence: No birth record survives. Modern estimates run c. 1180 to c. 1190; the traditional 1182 or 1185 is a back-calculation from his reported age, not a document, and 1 January is a placeholder. The pin is Magione town centre, which absorbed the locality of Pian del Carpine; the dossier's 43.1339, 12.2115 sits about 2.5 km toward the lake and disagrees with its own later entries, so one point is used throughout.
stops.campa: Between Lake Trasimeno and Perugia lies a scatter of Umbrian farmland called Pian del Carpine, the hornbeam plain, and here a boy is born whom nobody writes down. He will cross Asia and come back, and still no document will fix the year he began. The order he will carry into Germany does not exist yet; in that decade a cloth merchant's son in Assisi, a day's walk east, is himself still a boy. What the record gives instead of a date is the country: a few miles of Umbria, hornbeam and vine, the lake lying flat and shallow to the west.
suggested_refs: The monument to Plano Carpini at Magione, and the 780th-anniversary conference on his legacy held at Magione town hall, 5-6 June 2026, organized with the Mongolian University of Science and Technology
sources: Wikipedia, 'Giovanni da Pian del Carpine'
Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Giovanni da Pian del Carpine'
Conference program PDF, provincia.perugia.it

stops.name: Assisi, the chapter that sends the friars north
stops.date_confidence: Attested in Jordan of Giano's Chronica, which he dictated at the chapter of German Franciscans at Halberstadt in 1262. This is Giovanni's first securely dated appearance in any record. The count of twenty-six friars is the traditional figure. The single surviving manuscript of Jordan breaks off at 1238 and can carry nothing of Giovanni's later life.
stops.campa: At the general chapter of the order, held at the Portiuncula on the thirtieth of May, Caesarius of Speyer picks his party for Germany. An earlier attempt there had collapsed, the friars taken for heretics because the only German word among them was ja. Giovanni of Pian del Carpine, somewhere near forty, with nothing documented behind him at all, is chosen with about twenty-six others, Jordan of Giano and Thomas of Celano among them. It is the first time any record holds him.
suggested_refs: Jordan of Giano, Chronica, dictated at the Halberstadt chapter, 1262
sources: Jordan of Giano, Chronica, as summarized in the research dossier
Wikipedia, 'Jordan of Giano'
Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani

stops.name: Trento, sent ahead of the party
stops.date_confidence: Jordan of Giano places the advance to Trento in the summer of 1221; no day is given and 1 June is a placeholder ordering the segment. [R] The chronicle text was not fetched directly in this pass and reaches the file through the dossier's summary.
stops.campa: Giovanni and Barnabas the German go ahead of the others to Trento, at the foot of the passes, to arrange the road and the welcome. This is the work he will do for twenty years: not preaching so much as making a route usable, finding out who will feed a column of barefoot men and who will call the watch. The main party comes over the Alps behind them, and from Trento the mission moves into Bavaria and then down the Rhine, planting houses at Wurzburg, Mainz, Worms, Speyer, Strasbourg, and Cologne.
suggested_refs: The Alpine passes above Trento, the order's road into German lands
sources: Jordan of Giano, Chronica, as summarized in the research dossier

stops.name: Speyer, custos of Saxony
stops.date_confidence: Attested for 1223 in Jordan of Giano and confirmed by Treccani's Dizionario Biografico. No month or day is recorded and the date defaults to 1 January. The pin is Speyer Cathedral; the dossier's 8.4325 falls in the town some 750 m west of it.
stops.campa: At the provincial chapter held at Speyer, Albert of Pisa gives him the custody of Saxony, the raw northern edge of the province. The houses there are two years old at most, often a rented room and a borrowed altar. It is country that has to be crossed, and he crosses it. A Franciscan notice from these years calls him vir gravis et corpulentus, a heavy and corpulent man, and says he used a donkey while preaching in Germany, against the stricter walking ideal the order will argue over for a century.
suggested_refs: Speyer Cathedral, where the German province held its chapter in 1223
sources: Jordan of Giano, Chronica, as summarized in the research dossier
Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani

stops.name: Wurzburg, relieved of the custody
stops.date_confidence: Attested for 1224 in Jordan of Giano as summarized in the dossier; the chapter's month is not recorded and the date defaults to 1 January. [R] on the underlying chronicle text, not fetched in this pass.
stops.campa: At the chapter of Wurzburg he is taken off the Saxon custody and sent to Cologne. Jordan of Giano, who is in the room, gives the fact and withholds the reason. Franciscan administration in these years moves men the way a campaign moves them, quickly and without explanation, and the friars who keep the record think the explanation of no interest. A demotion, a reshuffle, or a promotion into a harder post? The chronicle does not say and no other document fills the gap.
suggested_refs: The Franciscan provincial chapter of Wurzburg, 1224
sources: Jordan of Giano, Chronica, as summarized in the research dossier

stops.name: Cologne, the custody on the Rhine
stops.date_confidence: The transfer is dated 1224 by Jordan of Giano as summarized in the dossier; the month is not recorded and June is a placeholder. [R] The 1224 appointment is not independently confirmed; the same pin's return-leg crossing of 1247 is.
stops.campa: He takes up the Cologne custody in a city with a cathedral chapter, a river, and money, all the things Saxony lacked. The friars here are moving into a permanent house, taking bequests, and beginning to look like an institution rather than a band of men sleeping in barns. He governs the district and keeps the accounts of a young order in a rich town, and hears the complaints of its guardians. Twenty-three years later he will cross this same river coming the other way, off the Asian steppe, with a khan's letter in his baggage.
suggested_refs: The early Franciscan house at Cologne, held under his custody from 1224
sources: Jordan of Giano, Chronica, as summarized in the research dossier
Wikipedia, 'Giovanni da Pian del Carpine'

stops.name: Cologne, minister provincial of Germany
stops.date_confidence: The appointment by minister general Giovanni Parenti is placed around 1228, the year of Francis's canonization on 16 July, which is the externally fixed anchor; the date of Giovanni's own appointment is not recorded. No seat is named for the German provincial in any source consulted, and the Cologne pin is an editorial placement. [R]
stops.campa: Giovanni Parenti, minister general, makes him minister provincial of all Germany in the year the order settles the argument over its founder by canonizing him. Francis is declared a saint at Assisi on the sixteenth of July 1228. Giovanni, who entered the order in Francis's lifetime and never once mentions him in anything that survives, is by then an administrator of provinces, responsible for every house between the Alps and the Baltic and for the friars sent to open more.
suggested_refs: The canonization of Francis of Assisi by Gregory IX, 16 July 1228
sources: Franciscan provincial records as summarized in the research dossier
Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani

stops.name: Spain, the provincialate
stops.date_confidence: The transfer to the Spanish province is placed at 1230 in the Franciscan administrative sequence summarized in the dossier. No month is recorded and no residence is named anywhere in the sources consulted. The Burgos coordinate is an editorial placement standing for a province, not an attested address. [R]
stops.campa: He is moved out of Germany altogether and sent to govern the Spanish province, and of the two years he spends there almost nothing survives: no letter, no foundation, no quarrel. It is the first of several stretches where the record simply thins out. By the time he is fifty the order has posted him over the Alps, down the Rhine, into Saxony and across the Pyrenees, and it keeps sending him into countries he does not know. Where he lived during the two Spanish years is recorded nowhere.
suggested_refs: The Franciscan province of Spain in the generalate of Giovanni Parenti
sources: Franciscan administrative sequence as summarized in the research dossier

stops.name: Metz, the Saxon province reaches into Lotharingia
stops.date_confidence: Treccani places the foundation of the Metz convent during his tenure as minister provincial of Saxony, 1232 to 1239. The dossier's date of 1230 contradicts this and is rejected: in 1230 he was being sent to Spain. The year here opens the tenure; the convent's actual year within that span is not fixed.
stops.campa: Elias of Cortona becomes minister general and Giovanni goes north again, this time over the newly cut province of Saxony, which he holds for seven years. Seven years of visitation, chapters and foundations leave almost no personal trace: a name at the head of documents, and not one sentence in his own voice. The convent at Metz is founded or supported somewhere in that stretch, one house among many in a province growing eastward faster than anyone can staff it.
suggested_refs: The Franciscan convent at Metz, founded during the Saxon provincialate
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani
Franciscan institutional records as summarized in the research dossier

stops.name: Prague, the letter concerning Agnes of Bohemia
stops.date_confidence: The papal letter of 31 August 1234 addressed to Giovanni and Thomas of Celano is cited from the dossier's summary of the papal register; the register entry itself was not fetched in this pass. [R]
stops.campa: Gregory IX writes to him and to Thomas of Celano, Francis's first biographer and a companion from the crossing of 1221, about the women's community forming at Prague under Agnes, daughter of the king of Bohemia. His province has reached the Bohemian court, and in eleven years that court will send him east with letters and an escort. Two friars who went over the Alps together thirteen years earlier are now named together from the papal chancery, over a princess who has refused an emperor in order to live poor.
suggested_refs: The Convent of St Agnes in Prague and Gregory IX's letter of 31 August 1234
sources: Papal chancery document of 31 August 1234, cited in the research dossier

stops.name: Lyon, the letters and the Easter departure
stops.date_confidence: The departure on Easter day, 16 April 1245, is attested in Giovanni's own itinerary and independently corroborated. The letters are dated 13 and 25 March 1245 in the papal registers per the dossier, not refetched here. Sequence flagged: both letters and the departure precede the First Council of Lyon, which opened 28 June, so the council cannot have prompted the commissioning, as the dossier's chronology has it. For 1239 to 1245 there is no secure document for him at all.
stops.campa: For six years there is no secure document for him, and then he is standing in front of a pope. Innocent IV, driven out of Rome and holding his curia at Lyon, counts the cruelties of the Tatars in Hungary among the five wounds he means to set before the council he has summoned. On the thirteenth of March he issues Cum non solum homines, demanding an account of Mongol intentions; on the twenty-fifth, Cum simus super, to the Eastern churches. On Easter day the friar rides east carrying both. He is past sixty.
suggested_refs: Innocent IV's letters Cum non solum homines (13 March 1245) and Cum simus super (25 March 1245) in the papal registers
sources: Giovanni da Pian del Carpine, Historia Mongalorum, itinerary chapter
Wikipedia, 'Giovanni da Pian del Carpine'
Wikipedia, 'First Council of Lyon'

stops.name: Prague, the counsel of King Wenceslaus
stops.date_confidence: Carpini's own text confirms the consultation with the king of Bohemia for route advice; no date is given and May 1245 orders the segment. The pin is Prague Castle, the royal seat. The dossier's 50.0875, 14.4213 is the Old Town, not a court.
stops.campa: He goes first to Wenceslaus I of Bohemia, an old friend from the years when Giovanni governed the province that reached into his kingdom. Every stage after this is arranged the same way, one prince recommending the friars to the next, until the line of Christian princes runs out and the recommendations have to be paid for in furs. The king tells him to go through Poland and Rus rather than by any southern road, gives him letters, provisions and safe conduct, and hands him on to his kinsmen.
suggested_refs: The route through Poland and Rus, chosen on Bohemian advice over the southern roads
sources: Giovanni da Pian del Carpine, Historia Mongalorum, tr. Rockhill; depts.washington.edu/silkroad/texts/carpini.html

stops.name: Wroclaw, Benedict the Pole joins the mission
stops.date_confidence: The join at Wroclaw is attested in Carpini's itinerary and in Benedict's own dictated account; no date is given and June 1245 is a placeholder ordering the route. Pin corrected to the cathedral on Ostrow Tumski; the dossier's coordinate lay some 550 m southwest near the Rynek.
stops.campa: At Wroclaw a Polish friar named Benedict joins as companion and interpreter in the Slav languages. He is the only man in the party who will be able to speak to anyone between here and the Volga. Benedict dictates his own short account afterward, De itinere Fratrum Minorum ad Tartaros, so that for everything that follows there are two witnesses who were there and can be set against each other, which is not true of much medieval travel writing. He rides at Giovanni's shoulder for the next two years.
suggested_refs: Benedict the Pole, De itinere Fratrum Minorum ad Tartaros, the mission's second witness
sources: Wikipedia, 'Benedict the Pole'
Giovanni da Pian del Carpine, Historia Mongalorum, tr. Rockhill

stops.name: Leczyca, the pelts of Conrad of Mazovia
stops.date_confidence: Carpini's itinerary names the meeting with Duke Conrad on the route; no date is recorded and July 1245 orders the segment.
stops.campa: Duke Conrad of Mazovia gives them beaver skins and other pelts. The friars are not carrying trade goods, they are carrying currency: among Mongol and Rus officials nobody is received without a present, and a papal legate who arrives empty-handed will be left standing outside the tent while his letters go unread. Giovanni learns the rule this early, on Christian ground, and is still complaining about it in writing two years later. The furs go into the saddlebags alongside the pope's two letters.
suggested_refs: The gift economy of the Mongol and Rus courts, as the friars encountered it
sources: Silk Road Seattle transcription of Rockhill's Carpini, 'Lenczy: Met Duke Conrad'

stops.name: Volodymyr-Volynskyi, briefed by Vasilko
stops.date_confidence: Carpini's account places the stay with Vasilko of Volhynia in late 1245, before the winter crossing to Kyiv; no date is given and November orders the segment. Volodymyr-Volynskyi is the traditional seat used here as a map point; Giovanni names no building and the exact site within Vasilko's territory is not specified.
stops.campa: Prince Vasilko, brother of Daniel of Galicia, has already dealt with the Mongols and knows exactly what the friars are riding into. He briefs them, keeps them through part of the winter, and sends word ahead along the road. His country has been ash for four years. The advice he gives is about presents: an ambassador who arrives with nothing concludes nothing, and the asking will be importunate and repeated. Giovanni writes the counsel down and repeats it afterward in almost the same words.
suggested_refs: The Galician-Volhynian principality four years after the Mongol conquest
sources: Giovanni da Pian del Carpine, Historia Mongalorum, tr. Rockhill
Wikipedia, 'Giovanni da Pian del Carpine'

stops.name: Danilov, ill to the point of death
stops.date_confidence: Carpini places the illness at Danilov before Kyiv, on the outbound leg in the winter of 1245 to 1246; no date is given and 1 January is a placeholder. The place cannot be securely located and the coordinate is a rough placement in Volhynia, not a confirmed site. [R]
stops.campa: At a place he calls Danilov the old friar falls ill enough to die. He does not stop. He has himself put in a cart and carried on through deep snow and bitter frost, because the mission has a season to keep and no way to send word ahead that it is delayed. Nobody in the party can turn back alone and nobody can be spared to nurse him. Whatever the sickness was, the account gives it a line and a half in the first person and then moves on to the next stage of the road, which is Kyiv.
stops.quote: Before we reached Kiew, when in Danilov, I was ill to the point of death
stops.quote_source: Giovanni da Pian del Carpine, Historia Mongalorum, tr. W. W. Rockhill (Hakluyt Society, 1900); transcribed at depts.washington.edu/silkroad/texts/carpini.html
suggested_refs: The unlocated Danilov of the outbound winter road
sources: Silk Road Seattle transcription of Rockhill's Carpini

stops.name: Kyiv, the horses changed
stops.date_confidence: Carpini's text reads 'on the second day after the feast of the Purification of Our Lady (February 4, 1246), we started out from Kiew.' The dossier's 3 February is an inclusive-count variant and is rejected here. The Lavra pin is a representative Kyiv site; the text names no building.
stops.campa: Kyiv has been rubble for five years, and the men who advise the friars there know the one thing that will decide whether they live: a Western horse cannot feed itself in a Mongol winter. A steppe pony breaks the crust with its hoof and grazes what is underneath; a Latin animal stands in the snow and starves. They leave the city two days after Candlemas with an escort, into country where the pope's name means nothing whatever. Their own horses stay behind in Kyiv, and they ride out on Mongol ones.
suggested_refs: Kyiv five years after the sack of 1240, on both legs of the embassy
sources: Silk Road Seattle transcription of Rockhill's Carpini
Wikipedia, 'Giovanni da Pian del Carpine'

segments.name: Into the Camps of the Tartars

stops.name: Kaniv, the first Mongol town, and Stephen left behind
stops.date_confidence: Carpini names Kaniv as the first Tartar-ruled town after Kyiv; the day is not given and 6 February orders the segment. Contradiction flagged and not resolved: the dossier puts Stephen of Bohemia's collapse at Batu's Volga camp, while Wikipedia and Treccani both place it at Kaniv near Kyiv, and Benedict's article says he was made to stay in a camp in Coman territory. The earlier siting is followed here.
stops.campa: Kaniv is the first town on the road held directly by the Mongols. Fresh horses and an escort are provided at once, and from this point the friars travel as guests of the empire, which is to say as its property, moved post to post at a speed no Christian courier in Europe could match. It is also where Stephen of Bohemia stops. He has come from Lyon at Giovanni's side and he cannot go on. He is left behind with the servants, and the other two ride east.
suggested_refs: The Mongol post system, ridden by the friars from Kaniv onward
sources: Silk Road Seattle transcription of Rockhill's Carpini
Wikipedia, 'Benedict the Pole'
Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani

stops.name: Corenza's camp, the Alan and the presents
stops.date_confidence: The reception by Corenza is attested in Carpini; no date is recorded and 20 February orders the route. The camp's location is not fixed in any source and the coordinate is an approximate placement on the Dnieper-Don steppe. [R]
stops.campa: The commander the friars call Corenza receives them on the open steppe, and his officer Micheas, an Alan, explains what protocol requires and how much of it. Some of what he says is invented. The presents are handed over anyway. Giovanni writes the whole transaction down, the false claims and the pelts both, with no moralizing about dishonesty and considerable irritation at the expense. The account itemizes what it cost and never says whether he believed Micheas.
suggested_refs: The Alan prefect Micheas, named in Carpini's account of the frontier camps
sources: Silk Road Seattle transcription of Rockhill's Carpini

stops.name: The Don, crossing east
stops.date_confidence: The crossing of the Don is a reconstruction from the general route geography; no crossing point is named in Giovanni's text and 1 March is a placeholder for the late-winter stage. [R]
stops.campa: They cross the Don going east on post-horses, changing mounts wherever the empire keeps them, five and six times in a day, riding through the wreckage of Comania. What they are crossing is not wilderness; it is a country recently emptied, and the roads through it work better than the roads in France, because one authority runs the whole length of them and can hang a man for stopping a courier. Giovanni notes the skulls and the bones lying about on the open ground.
suggested_refs: Comania after the Mongol conquest, described in the Historia Mongalorum
sources: Route geography as synthesized in the research dossier
Silk Road Seattle transcription of Rockhill's Carpini

stops.name: Batu's camp, between two fires
stops.date_confidence: Attested: Carpini reaches Batu on 'Wednesday in Holy Week (4th April)' 1246, sharper than the dossier's 'April 1246.' The pin approximates a seasonal ordu on the lower Volga rather than a fixed site, since Mongol camps moved; the source's own wording places it on the borders of the Comans' country.
stops.campa: They reach Batu in Holy Week, on the borders of the Comans' country by the Volga. Before anyone will look at the pope's letters the friars are walked between two fires with their gifts, and Giovanni asks what it is for. Because you may be carrying poison, he is told, or thinking something injurious to our lord, and the fire takes all harm out of it. He agrees. He will refuse to bow to an idol and refuse to bow to the south, and does refuse both, but a fire he can walk through.
stops.quote: Fear not, we only make you pass between these two fires lest perchance you think something injurious to our lord, or if you carry some poison, for the fire will remove all harm.
stops.quote_source: Giovanni da Pian del Carpine, Historia Mongalorum, Book I, tr. W. W. Rockhill (Hakluyt Society, 1900); depts.washington.edu/silkroad/texts/carpini.html
suggested_refs: The Mongol purification rite of passing between two fires, as reported by an eyewitness who submitted to it
sources: Silk Road Seattle transcription of Rockhill's Carpini
Wikipedia, 'Giovanni da Pian del Carpine'

stops.name: Batu's camp, the letters read and the friars sent on
stops.date_confidence: Carpini's next chapter opens 'On Holy Saturday (7th April) we were called to his tent'; the translation of the letters and the order to ride further east follow within days, and 8 April orders that sequence.
stops.campa: On Holy Saturday they are called into the tent. The papal letters are put into Ruthenian, Saracen and Tartar script and read out to Batu, who sits raised on a throne with one of his wives, his brothers and sons on a bench below him and everyone else on the ground. He hears them, and orders the friars sent on to the emperor himself, in Mongolia, two and a half thousand miles further east. The portrait Giovanni writes of him afterward is not a hostile one.
stops.quote: He is, however, most cruel in fight; he is very shrewd and extremely crafty in warfare, for he has been waging war for a long time.
stops.quote_source: Giovanni da Pian del Carpine, Historia Mongalorum, Book I ch. XII, on Batu, tr. W. W. Rockhill (Hakluyt Society, 1900); depts.washington.edu/silkroad/texts/carpini.html
suggested_refs: Batu Khan's ordu on the lower Volga, the western capital of the Mongol world
sources: Silk Road Seattle transcription of Rockhill's Carpini

segments.name: Three Thousand Miles in a Hundred and Six Days

stops.name: The Yaik, riding out of Batu's country
stops.date_confidence: The crossing of the Yaik (Ural) river system is reconstructed from the general route geography; no crossing point is named in the text and 12 April orders the segment. [R]
stops.campa: East of Batu's ordu the rivers of the Yaik mark the edge of anything the friars have a frame for. Beyond them there is no prince who has heard of a pope, no bishop, no road leading anywhere they can name to a man at home. They ride with a Mongol escort at the empire's own courier pace, changing horses at the posts, in the saddle from before dawn until deep in the night, and nobody adjusts the pace for two elderly friars. They are given a little millet and no bread.
suggested_refs: The Yaik (Ural) river system, edge of Batu's ulus on the eastward road
sources: Route geography as synthesized in the research dossier

stops.name: The Cangitae desert, Easter to Ascension
stops.date_confidence: Attested: Carpini rides this leg from 16 April to near the Ascension, 1246. The coordinate is an approximate placement in the Qangli zone and not a site named in the text.
stops.campa: The country of the Cangitae is desert and badly short of water, and the friars are a month crossing it. Few people live there; those who do live along the streams, and the friars ride between the water and the next water with an escort that knows where it is. Giovanni has no way to hand a Latin reader the size of the place, no map and no agreed measure of a day's ride across open ground. So he gives feast days instead, one dated stage after the next, out from Easter and on to near the Ascension of 1246.
suggested_refs: The Qangli desert leg, dated by Carpini from 16 April to near the Ascension 1246
sources: Silk Road Seattle transcription of Rockhill's Carpini

stops.name: The land of the Bisermins, towns standing empty
stops.date_confidence: Carpini travels this leg from the feast of the Ascension, 17 May, to about eight days before the feast of Saint John the Baptist, roughly 16 June 1246. The dossier's end date of 24 June misreads Rockhill's parenthesis, which glosses the feast rather than the end of the stage.
stops.campa: The Bisermins speak Coman and keep the law of the Saracens, and their country is full of ruined towns and broken forts. The armies came through here a quarter of a century before the friars did, and Giovanni is riding through the result: walls left standing with nobody inside them, cities he names where somebody has given him a name to write. He records the emptiness stage by stage, as a traveller records a distance, and makes nothing of it beyond what it is. The crossing takes a month.
suggested_refs: The ruined Khwarazmian cities of the Bisermins, seen a generation after their destruction
sources: Silk Road Seattle transcription of Rockhill's Carpini

stops.name: Omyl, the new city, and the court that keeps a dead man's wives
stops.date_confidence: Carpini places the newly built city of Omyl and the orda of Ordu in the land of the Black Kitayans, crossed between mid-May and late June 1246; no day is given and 20 June orders the segment. The coordinate approximates the Emil valley and is not an archaeological point. The dossier mis-sited this passage at Guyuk's imperial court near Karakorum; it belongs here.
stops.campa: In the country of the Black Kitayans the friars pass a city the Mongols have just finished building, and the orda of Ordu, Batu's elder brother, which is governed by one of his wives. Giovanni sets down the rule underneath it: a prince's court is not broken up when he dies. It is kept, a woman is appointed over it, and the same presents keep arriving as arrived in his lifetime. He has been four months inside the empire and is already writing down how it holds itself together after a death.
stops.quote: For it is a custom among the Tartars that the courts of their princes and nobles are not broken up (on their death), but some women are always appointed who govern them, and the same proportion of presents are given them that their lord had been in the habit (during his life) of allowing them.
stops.quote_source: Giovanni da Pian del Carpine, Historia Mongalorum, Book I ch. XVII, on the orda of Ordu in the land of the Black Kitayans, tr. W. W. Rockhill (Hakluyt Society, 1900); the transcription at depts.washington.edu/silkroad/texts/carpini.html carries an OCR slip, 'riot' for 'not', repaired here
suggested_refs: The orda of Ordu, elder brother of Batu, governed by his wife in the land of the Black Kitayans
sources: Silk Road Seattle transcription of Rockhill's Carpini

stops.name: Naiman country, snow on the twenty-ninth of June
stops.date_confidence: Attested: Carpini records a great snowfall on 29 June 1246 in Naiman territory, in mountainous country.
stops.campa: In the mountains of the Naimans, on the twenty-ninth of June, a great snow falls. The friars have been riding since Easter and are now high in the Altai in the middle of summer, in weather that would count as hard in a European January. Giovanni records it as a fact about the country and not as a wonder, which is how he treats every strange thing he has actually seen; the wonders in his book are all things other men told him. Three weeks of this lie between here and Mongolia proper.
suggested_refs: The Altai crossing of June 1246, snow recorded in high summer
sources: Silk Road Seattle transcription of Rockhill's Carpini

stops.name: Sira Orda, arrival on the feast of Mary Magdalene
stops.date_confidence: Attested: arrival at the Sira Orda on 22 July 1246, the feast of Mary Magdalene, after roughly three thousand miles in a hundred and six days. The pin is the canonical Karakorum coordinate; the imperial camp lay in that vicinity and was not the walled city itself, a caution the dossier makes explicitly.
stops.campa: On the twenty-second of July, the feast of Mary Magdalene, the friars ride into the Sira Orda, the Yellow Camp, in the grassland near Karakorum. They have covered about three thousand miles in a hundred and six days on borrowed horses, on millet and melted snow. Guyuk has not yet been raised. By an accident of timing they have come into the one interval when the whole empire gathers at a single place, the gap between one Great Khan and the next. Envoys are still riding in from every direction.
suggested_refs: The Sira Orda, the imperial camp in the Orkhon grassland near Karakorum
sources: Wikipedia, 'Giovanni da Pian del Carpine'
Silk Road Seattle transcription of Rockhill's Carpini

stops.name: The Golden Orda, the enthronement
stops.date_confidence: Attested: the enthronement on 24 August 1246, the feast of Saint Bartholomew, after hail forced the postponement of the intended day, 15 August. The scene belongs at the Golden Orda, three or four leagues from the Sira Orda by Carpini's own text; the dossier's attribution of it to the Sira Orda is wrong and is corrected here. The coordinate approximates that short remove.
stops.campa: The whole camp shifts three or four leagues, to a plain by a river between mountains, to a tent they call the Golden Orda. The assembly is to raise Ogedei's son. Hail on the fifteenth of August drives them off; on the twenty-fourth they do it. Thousands stand outside, princes and envoys out of Rus and Georgia and the caliph's Baghdad, and inside the chiefs go down on their knees, and then the whole people. Two friars out of Umbria and Poland stay standing, and nobody makes them kneel.
stops.quote: After doing this for a long while, they went back to the tent, and placed Cuyuc on the imperial seat, and the chiefs knelt before him; and after that the whole people did likewise, except ourselves who were not his subjects.
stops.quote_source: Giovanni da Pian del Carpine, Historia Mongalorum, Book II ch. IV, tr. W. W. Rockhill (Hakluyt Society, 1900); depts.washington.edu/silkroad/texts/carpini.html (a spaced semicolon in the transcription is closed up here)
suggested_refs: The Golden Orda, the second camp three or four leagues from the Sira Orda, where Guyuk was enthroned
sources: Silk Road Seattle transcription of Rockhill's Carpini
Wikipedia, 'Giovanni da Pian del Carpine'

stops.name: The imperial camp, Cosmas the goldsmith and what lies north
stops.date_confidence: The informants and the friars' hunger are attested in Carpini's own account, which gives no dates for them; September 1246 orders the segment. The dog-face passages in chapters V, IX and XIV are reported speech, marked in the text itself as hearsay ('are said to have'), and the places in them are places Giovanni never saw. [R] on the reported geography, [A] on the fact that he reported it. The placing of his report inside the older Latin cynocephalus tradition is likewise [R]: he cites no authority for the motif and names no source but his informants.
stops.campa: A Russian goldsmith named Cosmas, who made Guyuk's throne and cut his seal, feeds them: the ration issued for four is barely enough for one, and the papal legates are starving in the middle of an imperial festival. From Cosmas, from Rus clerics and from men held here for years, Giovanni takes down the empire's history and its map, out past the last people anyone has been to. Told of men with dog faces along the northern ocean, he writes it as told, with the distancing phrase, and the report lands on a Latin shelf where Ctesias and Solinus have kept dog-headed peoples for centuries.
stops.quote: After the Bascarts, the Parrosits, and the Samogeds, after the Samogeds those who are said to have dog-faces, who live in the deserts along the coasts of the Ocean.
stops.quote_source: Giovanni da Pian del Carpine, Historia Mongalorum, ch. XIV, tr. W. W. Rockhill (Hakluyt Society, 1900); depts.washington.edu/silkroad/texts/carpini.html
suggested_refs: Benedict the Pole's independent list of the Cynocephali beyond the Bashkirs
Martin Waldseemuller's Carta marina of 1516, which draws dog-headed figures into Tartaria with a caption on speech broken by barking, per Chet Van Duzer's work on the map's long legends
sources: Silk Road Seattle transcription of Rockhill's Carpini
Benedict the Pole, De itinere Fratrum Minorum ad Tartaros

stops.name: The imperial camp, the death of Yaroslav
stops.date_confidence: Carpini reports the death of Yaroslav of Vladimir-Suzdal at the imperial orda during the friars' stay; the exact day is not given and 20 September orders the segment. Giovanni reports the poisoning as what was believed, not as established fact, and the wording preserves that.
stops.campa: Yaroslav, grand duke of Suzdal, is invited to the tent of the emperor's mother and given food and drink from her own hand, as an honour. He goes back to his lodging, falls ill, and is dead in seven days, his whole body strangely livid. Giovanni is at a court where he cannot ask a question and cannot leave, and he is eating that court's rations while he writes. He sets the death down as it reached him, with the belief attached rather than a verdict: so that everyone believed that he had been poisoned.
stops.quote: It happened that he was invited by the mother of the Emperor (to her tent), and she gave him to eat and drink with her own hand, as if to honour him; and he went back to his lodgings straightway and fell ill, and after seven days he was dead, and all his body became livid in strange fashion; so that everyone believed that he had been poisoned.
stops.quote_source: Giovanni da Pian del Carpine, Historia Mongalorum, tr. W. W. Rockhill (Hakluyt Society, 1900); depts.washington.edu/silkroad/texts/carpini.html
suggested_refs: Yaroslav II of Vladimir-Suzdal, dead at the Mongol imperial court in 1246
sources: Silk Road Seattle transcription of Rockhill's Carpini

stops.name: The imperial camp, the khan's letter checked word by word
stops.date_confidence: Attested for 11 November 1246 in Carpini's account of the translation session, with the Rus goldsmith Cosmas and a clerk named Temer assisting. The dossier reports the surviving Persian text with the Mongol seal as held in the Vatican Apostolic Archives; that holding was not independently verified in this pass. [R] on the archival location.
stops.campa: On the eleventh of November the officials sit the friars down and go through the emperor's answer word by word, Latin against Mongol, checking that nothing has slipped in the rendering. The letter does not reply to the pope's complaint. It orders the pope and the kings of the West to come in person and submit, and it asks how the pope knows whom God forgives. No document of the Mongol empire has ever reached a European chancery. Giovanni packs this one into his own baggage for the ride west.
suggested_refs: Guyuk's letter to Innocent IV, the Persian text with the Mongol seal, reported in the Vatican Apostolic Archives
sources: Silk Road Seattle transcription of Rockhill's Carpini
Guyuk's letter to Innocent IV, as summarized in the research dossier

stops.name: The imperial camp, leave to go and the fox-skin gowns
stops.date_confidence: Attested: 13 November 1246, the feast of Saint Brice, in Carpini's own text, which gives the leave, the sealed letter and the gifts in a single sentence.
stops.campa: On the feast of Saint Brice they are given leave to go, and the emperor's letter under seal, and sent to his mother, who gives each of them a fox-skin gown with the fur outside and a piece of purple cloth. Their own Mongol escort steals a hand's breadth off each piece on the road, and more than half of the servant's. Giovanni watches it happen and says nothing, and then writes down both facts, the theft and his own silence, in one sentence, without excusing either.
stops.quote: ...they sent us to the Emperor's mother, who gave to each of us a fox-skin gown with the fur outside and wadding inside, and also a piece of purple, of which our Tartars stole a palm's length from each, and also more than half of another piece which was given to our servant; but though it was no secret to us, we did not choose to make any ado over it.
stops.quote_source: Giovanni da Pian del Carpine, Historia Mongalorum, Book II ch. XIII, tr. W. W. Rockhill (Hakluyt Society, 1900); depts.washington.edu/silkroad/texts/carpini.html (an OCR hyphen in 'purple-of' is repaired here)
suggested_refs: Toregene, mother of Guyuk, who gave the departing legates their travelling furs
sources: Silk Road Seattle transcription of Rockhill's Carpini
Wikipedia, 'Giovanni da Pian del Carpine'

stops.name: The steppe, sleeping under the snow
stops.date_confidence: The return crossing runs from November 1246 to May 1247; its stages carry no dates and 15 December is a placeholder. The coordinate is a generic placement on the return route, not a named site. [R]
stops.campa: They ride west the whole winter, sleeping in the open on snow, scraping a bare place with their feet where there are no trees, waking under a drift. There is nobody ahead to send word to and nobody behind expecting them, and the escort that moves them has no interest in their comfort or their survival past the next post. The letter of the emperor of the Tartars to the bishop of Rome crosses Central Asia in the saddlebag of a man past sixty who is sleeping in a hollow he scraped with his boots.
stops.quote: We were travelling the whole winter, resting most of the time in the snow in the desert, save when in the open plain where there were no trees we could scrape a bare place with our feet; and often when the wind drifted it we would find (on waking) our bodies all covered with snow.
stops.quote_source: Giovanni da Pian del Carpine, Historia Mongalorum, Book III, on the route travelled coming back, tr. W. W. Rockhill (Hakluyt Society, 1900); depts.washington.edu/silkroad/texts/carpini.html
suggested_refs: The six-month winter return across the steppe, November 1246 to May 1247
sources: Silk Road Seattle transcription of Rockhill's Carpini

stops.name: Batu's camp, the Ascension
stops.date_confidence: Attested: Carpini reaches Batu again on the Ascension of our Lord, 9 May 1247. The pin is the same approximation of a seasonal lower-Volga ordu used on the outbound leg.
stops.campa: On the Ascension they are back at Batu's ordu on the Volga, six months out of Mongolia and about a year and a month since they last stood here. Batu lets them through. There is no second interrogation and no delay of the kind that held them on the way east; the empire has decided what it thinks of this embassy and has put the decision in writing under a seal these friars are carrying themselves. They are given an escort and sent on west, and the account moves straight to the next camp.
suggested_refs: Batu's ordu on the return leg, 9 May 1247
sources: Silk Road Seattle transcription of Rockhill's Carpini

stops.name: Mauci's camp, the servants recovered
stops.date_confidence: Carpini reaches Mauci 'on the Saturday after the octave of Pentecost (2nd June)' 1247. The dossier's 9 June is Kyiv's date shifted onto this stop and is corrected here. The camp's position is not fixed in any source and the coordinate is an approximation between the Volga and the Dnieper. [R] on the location.
stops.campa: At the camp of the commander Mauci they find their own companions and servants again, the men left behind on the outward road more than a year earlier and told to wait among strangers whose language they did not have. Nothing in the account says what those men did with the year, how they were fed, or whether they went on expecting anybody to come back for them. Giovanni gives them a clause. They are collected up, and for the first time since Kaniv the party is whole.
suggested_refs: The camp of Mauci (Moge), where the mission's servants had waited out the year
sources: Silk Road Seattle transcription of Rockhill's Carpini

stops.name: Kyiv, as if risen from the dead
stops.date_confidence: Carpini's text reads 'We reached (Kiew) fifteen days before the feast of Saint John the Baptist (9th June).' Wikipedia's 10 June is a defensible inclusive-count variant; 9 June, the date the translated text carries, is used here and the disagreement is left standing rather than resolved.
stops.campa: The Kyivans come out of the ruined city to meet them, rejoicing. Nobody in Rus, Poland or Bohemia has expected these men back; the embassy was written off somewhere past the Don eighteen months earlier and no word of it had come west since. The whole line of princes who handed him east had counted him among the dead and gone on with their business. The same greeting meets him at every stage of the road home, through Poland and Bohemia, and he writes it down each time: congratulated as if we had risen from the dead.
stops.quote: The Kiewians who had heard of our arrival all came out to meet us rejoicing, and congratulated us as if we had risen from the dead, and so they did to us throughout Ruscia, Poland and Bohemia.
stops.quote_source: Giovanni da Pian del Carpine, Historia Mongalorum, Book III ch. II, tr. W. W. Rockhill (Hakluyt Society, 1900); depts.washington.edu/silkroad/texts/carpini.html
suggested_refs: Kyiv on the return leg, 9 June 1247
sources: Silk Road Seattle transcription of Rockhill's Carpini
Wikipedia, 'Giovanni da Pian del Carpine'

stops.name: Volodymyr-Volynskyi, eight days held at table
stops.date_confidence: Carpini says Daniel and Vasilko kept them 'against our will, for quite eight days' after the return to Kyiv; no dates are given and 20 June orders the segment. Contradiction flagged on the quotation: the dossier assigns Vasilko's counsel about presents to the outward journey in 1245, while Rockhill's text carries it in Book III, immediately after the return to Kyiv. Not resolved here.
stops.campa: Daniel of Galicia and his brother Vasilko keep the friars at table for eight days and, Giovanni says, will not let them leave. Something has been decided in the year and a half the embassy was away. A principality that has already measured the Mongols is looking for a second patron: the two princes send envoys back with him to treat with the pope about the union of their church with Rome. The men who briefed him on the way out now want him to carry their own business west.
stops.quote: He told us that if we wanted to go to them we must have rich presents to give them, for they were in the habit of asking for them most importunately, and if they were not given them...an ambassador could not conduct his business satisfactorily with them.
stops.quote_source: Giovanni da Pian del Carpine, Historia Mongalorum, Book III ch. II, on the counsel of Duke Vassilko, tr. W. W. Rockhill (Hakluyt Society, 1900); depts.washington.edu/silkroad/texts/carpini.html
suggested_refs: The Galician-Volhynian embassy sent west with the friars in 1247
sources: Silk Road Seattle transcription of Rockhill's Carpini

stops.name: Cologne, crossing the Rhine
stops.date_confidence: The Rhine crossing at Cologne on the return leg is attested; no date is recorded, and 15 October is a placeholder between the Rus stages and the arrival at Lyon on 18 November.
stops.campa: He crosses the Rhine at Cologne, in the custody he governed twenty-three years earlier, and rides on south without stopping long. The friars there are looking at a man they last knew as an administrator of provinces, come back off the far side of the world with two companions, a set of furs stolen down at the edges, and a sealed letter in a script nobody in the house can read. The account gives the crossing a single clause. It does not stop for the reunion or record who was there.
suggested_refs: The Rhine crossing at Cologne, autumn 1247
sources: Wikipedia, 'Giovanni da Pian del Carpine'
Silk Road Seattle transcription of Rockhill's Carpini

stops.name: Lyon, the report delivered
stops.date_confidence: Attested: the friars reach Lyon and deliver Guyuk's letter and their report to Innocent IV on 18 November 1247. Note that the figure of three thousand miles in a hundred and six days belongs to the eastward ride across Asia, not to the whole embassy, which covered far more ground.
stops.campa: Two years and seven months after riding out, Giovanni comes back into Lyon and finds the pope still there. He hands over Guyuk's letter, which refuses everything that was asked and orders the pope to present himself, and with it his own book. The Historia Mongalorum is the first account of the Mongols written in Latin by a man who went, sat in the camp, ate the rations and counted the tents, and it keeps a visible line between what he saw and what he was told.
suggested_refs: The Historia Mongalorum quos nos Tartaros appellamus, delivered at Lyon in November 1247
sources: Wikipedia, 'Giovanni da Pian del Carpine'
Silk Road Seattle transcription of Rockhill's Carpini

segments.name: The Book, the Mitre, and the Last Document

stops.name: Lyon, penitentiary at the curia, and the book read aloud
stops.date_confidence: A papal document of 23 January 1248 names him penitentiary at the curia, an office he holds about three months; the document is cited from the dossier and was not refetched in this pass. Salimbene's meeting with him in France is placed in 1247 to 1248 and is not dated more closely. The C. de Bridia text is dated 30 July 1247 by its own colophon and is not Giovanni's work.
stops.campa: For three months he is a penitentiary at the papal court, and in those months the book goes into circulation under its author's own hand. Salimbene de Adam meets him in France and records what he saw: Giovanni carrying the volume about with him, letting men read it, and stopping to explain the passages that made them laugh or refuse to believe. Two recensions survive. The fuller one ends with a list of witnesses and a warning to copyists to add nothing.
suggested_refs: Salimbene de Adam, Cronica, on the author reading and explaining his own book in France
The Hystoria Tartarorum of C. de Bridia, colophon dated 30 July 1247, a related but separate text
sources: Salimbene de Adam, Cronica, as cited in the research dossier
Manuscript tradition of the Historia Mongalorum as described in the dossier

stops.name: France, the embassy to Louis IX
stops.date_confidence: Treccani attests an embassy to Louis IX of France in 1248; the purpose, possibly to urge postponement of the crusade during Innocent IV's war with Frederick II, is explicitly uncertain in every source. No source places the meeting in Paris: Louis spent 1248 preparing to sail and left for Aigues-Mortes that summer. The Paris coordinate is an editorial placement, not an attested location, and the month is a placeholder.
stops.campa: The pope sends him to the king of France. What he was told to say is nowhere recorded, and the sources that report the embassy say so plainly rather than guessing. Innocent IV is at war with an emperor and would rather the crusade waited; Louis has taken the cross and will not wait. No surviving document shows anyone asking the friar who stood in the ordu and counted what the empire could put in the field what he made of the odds. In the summer of 1248 the king sails for Egypt.
suggested_refs: Louis IX's departure for the Seventh Crusade, summer 1248
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani
Papal diplomatic record of the 1248 mission, as summarized in the research dossier

stops.name: Antivari, archbishop in Dalmatia
stops.date_confidence: The appointment is dated 1248 by Treccani and the Italian Wikipedia; the English Wikipedia's 'from 1247 to 1252' is the outlier and is not followed. No month is recorded and the date defaults to 1 January. The pin is Stari Bar, the medieval seat with the cathedral of St George, not the modern coastal town of Bar that the dossier's coordinate points to.
stops.campa: He is made archbishop of Antivari on the Adriatic coast of what is now Montenegro, a see whose primacy over Serbia is claimed and contested. It is the end of the career: a difficult province a long way from Lyon, given to a man in his sixties who has just made the hardest journey any Latin Christian has made. Nothing in the four years that follow has anything to do with the Mongols. He administers a small coastal diocese, a cathedral of St George at Stari Bar and a contested boundary.
suggested_refs: The cathedral of St George at Stari Bar, seat of the archbishops of Antivari
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani
Wikipedia, 'Giovanni da Pian del Carpine'

stops.name: Ragusa, the bishop's claim and the imprisonment
stops.date_confidence: The jurisdictional conflict with the bishop of Ragusa and Giovanni's capture and brief imprisonment are summarized from ecclesiastical records in the dossier and were not independently verified in this pass; no date is recorded and 1250 sits in the middle of the dispute. [R] There is no evidence of any criminal conviction.
stops.campa: The bishop of Ragusa claims Antivari as his own, and the quarrel goes far enough that the archbishop is seized and held. He is released. No charge, no conviction and no account of the terms survives. The man who was walked between two fires at Batu's tent and stayed on his feet while an empire knelt is taken prisoner by another Catholic bishop over a boundary line on the Adriatic. The dispute outlives the bishop, who dies in May 1252, and runs on into July.
suggested_refs: The Antivari-Ragusa jurisdictional dispute, closed in July 1252
sources: Ecclesiastical dispute records as summarized in the research dossier

stops.name: Antivari, the last document and the summer of 1252
stops.date_confidence: The last surviving document naming him is dated 29 July 1252. The Franciscan Martyrology gives 1 August 1252 for the death and Treccani has 'probably in the first days of August'; the day is conventional and not independently secure beyond the July document. No burial record, tomb, grave marker or local cult could be found in any source consulted, which is an attested absence and not a lost monument.
stops.campa: On the twenty-ninth of July 1252 a document names him for the last time. The Franciscan martyrology puts his death on the first of August, in his own diocese, about a month after the Ragusa quarrel was settled. No medieval source says where he was put in the ground, and no shrine or grave tradition grew at Bar. He had written the first Latin history of Chinggis Khan and the first eyewitness description of the Mongol court, and three and a half centuries later Hakluyt printed it in London without knowing where its author lay.
suggested_refs: Richard Hakluyt, The Principal Navigations (1598), the first printing; C. R. Beazley, The Texts and Versions of John de Plano Carpini and William de Rubruquis (Hakluyt Society, 1903)
Anastasius van den Wyngaert, Sinica Franciscana I (Quaracchi, 1929); Menesto, Lungarotti, Daffina and Petech, Storia dei Mongoli (Spoleto, 1989), the modern critical edition
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani
